name: Must Have
childIntro: Think carefully. Which one does it always have to have, every single time?
howItWorks: The sentence is usually all X must have blank, or X cannot happen without blank. It runs at OLSAT levels D through G. The distractors are things that are almost always present but not actually required, which is exactly the difference the question is testing.
parentTip: The test here is necessary versus merely typical. Teach the counterexample habit: for each choice ask, can I think of one that does not have this? A meal without friends is still a meal. A meal without food is not. One counterexample kills a choice.

questions.prompt: A meal cannot be eaten without —
questions.explanation: You can eat a meal with your hands, standing up, alone, straight from the pan. But you cannot eat a meal without food.
questions.strategy: For every choice, try to think of one example that does not have it. If you can, cross it off.

questions.explanation: Plenty of songs have no words, no guitar and no drums. Some are played, not sung. But every song is made of sound.
questions.strategy: Start with the choice that seems too obvious. It is often the right one.

questions.explanation: A lamp or a torch casts a shadow just as the sun does, so the sun is not required. A shadow can fall on the ground, not just a wall. But without any light there is no shadow at all.
questions.strategy: The most common answer is not always the necessary one. Sunlight is one kind of light.

questions.explanation: Many books have no pictures, no chapters and no index. Pages are the one thing a book cannot do without.
questions.strategy: Ask which choice would still leave you with a book if you removed it.

questions.explanation: Knots can be tied in wire, in hair, in a shoelace or in a plastic bag, so rope is not required. But whatever you tie must be able to bend and cross over itself.
questions.strategy: Replace a specific thing with the general idea behind it. Rope becomes something bendy.

questions.explanation: You can travel without a map, on foot, with nothing packed and never stay anywhere. But every journey starts somewhere.
questions.strategy: Necessary means it could not be otherwise. Typical means it usually is.

questions.explanation: Rain often comes with clouds, and clouds are how rain usually forms, but the one thing rain absolutely is made of is water. Thunder, wind and cold are all sometimes absent.
questions.strategy: Ask what the thing is MADE of. That is almost always necessary.

questions.explanation: Arguments can be calm and quiet, can end with nobody winning, and can happen among several people or inside one person's head. But without disagreement there is no argument.
questions.strategy: Strip away every feeling and detail. What is left is the definition.

questions.explanation: Promises need no handshake, no witness, no paper and no reward. What they do need is somebody saying they will do something later.
questions.strategy: Abstract words still have a core. Ask what would make it stop being that thing.

questions.explanation: You can measure without a ruler, without being a scientist, and without using metres. Measurements are often approximate. But a measurement with no unit is meaningless: five what?
questions.strategy: If a choice names one particular example of something, look for the general word instead.

questions.explanation: Many trees have no fruit, and a tree in winter has no leaves at all. Birds and shade come and go. But every tree draws water through roots.
questions.strategy: For each choice, try to think of one that does not have it. If you can, cross it off.

questions.prompt: A game cannot be played without —
questions.explanation: Games can be played alone, with no board, no ball, and can end in a draw with no winner. But without rules there is nothing to play.
questions.strategy: Start with the choice that sounds too obvious. It is often the necessary one.

questions.explanation: Letters can be carved, typed on a screen, or shaped in sand, so ink and paper are not needed. A single letter carries no meaning on its own. But a letter you cannot see the shape of is not a letter.
questions.strategy: Ask what would make the thing stop being that thing.

questions.explanation: A lamp casts shadows as well as the sun, and a shadow can fall on the ground, not just a wall. But something has to get in the way of the light.
questions.strategy: Replace a specific thing with the general idea behind it. Sun becomes light.

questions.explanation: Rivers can be empty of fish, have no bridges or boats, and run dead straight. But a river with no water is a dry bed, not a river.
questions.strategy: What the thing is MADE of is almost always necessary.

questions.explanation: Conversations can be rude, can wander with no clear topic, and can end in disagreement. They can even happen in sign language with no spoken words. But one person alone is not having a conversation.
questions.strategy: Some things need two of something. Check the number as well as the parts.

questions.explanation: Plenty of questions have no answer anyone knows. A spoken question has no question mark. But if nothing is unknown, it is not really a question.
questions.strategy: Strip away the writing and the speaking. What idea is left?

choices.text: a smaller scale than the place

questions.explanation: Maps come without colour, without roads, without a compass and without labels. What makes something a map is that it shows a place shrunk down.
questions.strategy: The definition is usually the thing you would never think to say out loud.

questions.explanation: A mirror is only one kind of reflecting surface; polished metal and still water work too. A reflection needs light, but light alone is not enough. Something has to bounce it back.
questions.strategy: When one choice names a specific example, look for the general word instead.

questions.explanation: Plans can live entirely in your head, have no deadline and involve nobody else. What every plan has is something you intend to do later.
questions.strategy: Look for the choice that is true even in the simplest possible example.

questions.explanation: Books exist without covers, chapters, indexes and even without a named author. But an object with nothing on the pages at all is a notebook, not a book.
questions.strategy: Remove each choice in turn. Which removal stops it being a book?

questions.explanation: Many songs have no words, no chorus and no instruments, and can be played rather than sung. But a song is made of sound.
questions.strategy: What the thing is made of is almost always the necessary part.

questions.explanation: Choices can be made in a split second, for no reason, with no clearly right answer. But with only one option there is nothing to choose.
questions.strategy: Ask what makes the word mean anything at all.

questions.explanation: You can measure without a ruler and without being a scientist. Measurements are often approximate, and inches work as well as metres. But five, on its own, means nothing. Five what?
questions.strategy: If a choice names one particular example, look for the general word instead.

questions.explanation: Plenty of recipes need no oven, give amounts as a handful or a pinch, carry no picture, and are cooked by anyone at home. But a recipe with nothing to cook is not a recipe.
questions.strategy: Cross off anything that is only usually true. Necessary means always.

questions.prompt: Every shadow puppet show must have —
questions.explanation: Puppets can be cut from card rather than made with hands, the story can be improvised, and a show can be rehearsed with nobody watching. But with no light there is no shadow.
questions.strategy: Trace the chain of causes back. What has to come first?

questions.explanation: Caves and valleys are only two of the places echoes happen. A quiet sound echoes too. But the sound must reflect off something.
questions.strategy: Two of the choices are specific places. Neither can be necessary if the other also works.

questions.explanation: Debates can be calm, private, unjudged and unamplified. But if everyone agrees, there is nothing to debate.
questions.strategy: Strip away every feeling and every prop. The definition is what remains.

questions.explanation: Translations can be done from memory, can be inaccurate, and can be of signs or symbols rather than words. But something has to move from one language into another.
questions.strategy: Count the parts. Some things need exactly two of something.

questions.explanation: Fossils can be footprints or leaf prints rather than bones, can be preserved in amber or tar rather than stone, and are usually incomplete. Most sit in the ground, not a museum. What makes something a fossil is that it is very old.
questions.strategy: When four choices are examples or places, the fifth is usually the definition.
